items.readable_text:
Content:
A complex number [MATH: z] is called an [MATH: n]th root of unity if it satisfies the equation
[MATH: z^n=1.]

Content:
(The word "unity" is simply another name for the number one.)

Content:
For example, to find all the 5th roots of unity, we must solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: z^5=1.]

Content:
We start by expressing the right-hand side in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm i\theta}.]

Content:
Computing the magnitude and argument of unity, we have

Content:
- [MATH: r = |1| = {\color{blue}1},] and
- [MATH: \theta = \arg(1) = {\color{red}{0}}.]

Content:
Now, here's the trick. When expressing unity in exponential form, we add an arbitrary integer multiple of [MATH: 2\pi,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1|= re^{\textrm{i}θ}; = re^{\textrm{i}(θ + 2kπ)}; = 1 ⋅ e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2kπ)}; = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}]

Content:
where [MATH: k] is an integer.

Content:
Now, rewriting the right-hand side of the equation [MATH: z^5 = 1,] we get

Content:
[MATH: z^5 = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
Taking the 5th root of both sides gives

Content:
[MATH: z_{k} = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/5} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/5}.]

Content:
There are exactly [MATH: 5] distinct 5th roots of unity. To find these, we substitute [MATH: k=0] up to [MATH: k=4] into the above, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: k = 0|: z_{0} = e^{2(0)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{0} = 1; k = 1|: z_{1} = e^{2(1)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{2π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 2|: z_{2} = e^{2(2)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{4π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 3|: z_{3} = e^{2(3)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 4|: z_{4} = e^{2(4)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{8π\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
Therefore, our 5th roots of unity are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \quad e^{2\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{4\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{6\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{8\pi\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
In general, the case corresponding to [MATH: k=1] is the principal [MATH: n]th root of unity. So, the principal [MATH: 5]th root of unity is

Content:
[MATH: z_1 = e^{2\pi \textrm{i}/5}.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the principal [MATH: 6]th root of unity.
sections.readable_text: Find the principal [MATH: 6]th root of unity.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: z] be a [MATH: 6]th root of unity. This means that

[MATH: z^{6} = 1.]

First, we express the complex number [MATH: 1] in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}.] Notice that [MATH: |1| = 1] and [MATH: \arg(1) = 0.] Hence,

[MATH: 1 = e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2k\pi)} = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}},]

where [MATH: k] is an integer. So, we have

[MATH: z^{6} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}⟹z = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/6} = e^{kπ\textrm{i}/3}.]

The principal root corresponds to [MATH: k=1,] and is therefore equal to [MATH: e^{\pi \textrm{i}/3}.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the root of unity highlighted in the diagram below.
sections.readable_text:
Find the root of unity highlighted in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/98e9ea0ab66a999ba39a7d107f156d9f]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The [MATH: n]th roots of unity lie at the vertices of a regular [MATH: n]-gon inscribed inside the unit circle in the complex plane. One of the vertices of this regular [MATH: n]-gon must lie at the point [MATH: (1,0).]

Since there are [MATH: 7] points in our diagram, we need to find a [MATH: 7]th root of unity.

First, we express the complex number [MATH: 1] in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}.] Notice that [MATH: |1| = 1] and [MATH: \arg(1) = 0.] Hence,

[MATH: 1 = e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2k\pi)} = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}},]

where [MATH: k] is an integer. So, we have

[MATH: z^{7} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}⟹z = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/7} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/7}.]

To find the index [MATH: k] of our root of unity, we enumerate the roots in the diagram counter-clockwise, starting with the root at [MATH: (1,0)] corresponding to [MATH: k=0,] as shown below.

So, the required root corresponds to [MATH: k=5.] Substituting this into the expression for roots, we obtain the following:

[MATH: z_{5} = e^{2(5)π\textrm{i}/7} = e^{10π\textrm{i}/7}]

Content:
Earlier, when finding the 5th roots of unity, we substituted the integers from [MATH: k=0] to [MATH: k=4] inclusive into the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: z_{k} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
This process gave us the following results:

Content:
[MATH: z_0 = 1, \qquad z_1 = e^{2\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_2 = e^{4\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_3 = e^{6\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_4 = e^{8\pi\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
You may be wondering why we stopped at [MATH: k=4.] What about [MATH: k=5,6,7,\ldots?]

Content:
It turns out that if we continue substituting values for [MATH: k,] we'll get the same results repeated. In other words, we will not get any other roots.

Content:
For example, substituting [MATH: k=8] into our formula gives

Content:
[MATH: z_{8}|= e^{2(8)π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{16π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5 + 10π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5 + 2π\textrm{i}}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5} ⋅ e^{2π\textrm{i}}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5} ⋅ 1; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5}; = z_{3}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A complex number [MATH: z] is called an [MATH: n]th root of unity if it satisfies the equation
[MATH: z^n=1.]

Content:
(The word "unity" is simply another name for the number one.)

Content:
For example, to find all the 5th roots of unity, we must solve the equation

Content:
[MATH: z^5=1.]

Content:
We start by expressing the right-hand side in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm i\theta}.]

Content:
Computing the magnitude and argument of unity, we have

Content:
- [MATH: r = |1| = {\color{blue}1},] and
- [MATH: \theta = \arg(1) = {\color{red}{0}}.]

Content:
Now, here's the trick. When expressing unity in exponential form, we add an arbitrary integer multiple of [MATH: 2\pi,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1|= re^{\textrm{i}θ}; = re^{\textrm{i}(θ + 2kπ)}; = 1 ⋅ e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2kπ)}; = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}]

Content:
where [MATH: k] is an integer.

Content:
Now, rewriting the right-hand side of the equation [MATH: z^5 = 1,] we get

Content:
[MATH: z^5 = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}}.]

Content:
Taking the 5th root of both sides gives

Content:
[MATH: z_{k} = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/5} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/5}.]

Content:
There are exactly [MATH: 5] distinct 5th roots of unity. To find these, we substitute [MATH: k=0] up to [MATH: k=4] into the above, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: k = 0|: z_{0} = e^{2(0)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{0} = 1; k = 1|: z_{1} = e^{2(1)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{2π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 2|: z_{2} = e^{2(2)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{4π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 3|: z_{3} = e^{2(3)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5}; k = 4|: z_{4} = e^{2(4)π\textrm{i}/5} = e^{8π\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
Therefore, our 5th roots of unity are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \quad e^{2\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{4\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{6\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \quad e^{8\pi\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
In general, the case corresponding to [MATH: k=1] is the principal [MATH: n]th root of unity. So, the principal [MATH: 5]th root of unity is

Content:
[MATH: z_1 = e^{2\pi \textrm{i}/5}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding Primary Roots of Unity

Example Prompt:
Find the principal [MATH: 6]th root of unity.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: z] be a [MATH: 6]th root of unity. This means that

[MATH: z^{6} = 1.]

First, we express the complex number [MATH: 1] in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}.] Notice that [MATH: |1| = 1] and [MATH: \arg(1) = 0.] Hence,

[MATH: 1 = e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2k\pi)} = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}},]

where [MATH: k] is an integer. So, we have

[MATH: z^{6} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}⟹z = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/6} = e^{kπ\textrm{i}/3}.]

The principal root corresponds to [MATH: k=1,] and is therefore equal to [MATH: e^{\pi \textrm{i}/3}.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Geometry of the Nth Roots of Unity

Content:
Earlier, we found that the [MATH: 5]th roots of unity are as follows:

Content:
[MATH: z_0 = 1, \qquad z_1 = e^{2\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_2 = e^{4\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_3 = e^{6\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_4 = e^{8\pi\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
All five roots lie on the unit circle in the complex plane and form a regular pentagon, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ec13de4c6c3d50e17c6a7c19dc5890de]

Content:
In general, the [MATH: n]th roots of unity will always lie on the unit circle in the complex plane, and its vertices are those of a regular [MATH: n]-gon. Moreover,

Content:
- [MATH: z_0 = 1] is always a vertex of this polygon, and
- if [MATH: n] is even, then [MATH: z_{n/2} = -1] is also a vertex of this polygon.

---

Item 6 — Example: Geometric Interpretation of the Roots of Unity

Example Prompt:
Sketch a diagram showing all the [MATH: 4]th roots of unity.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Geometrically, the [MATH: 4]th roots of unity have the following properties:

- all of them lie on the unit circle centered in the origin,
- one of the roots is [MATH: 1,] corresponding to the point [MATH: (1,0)] on the complex plane,
- the roots form a square (regular [MATH: 4]-sided polygon).

Item 9 — Example: Finding Roots of Unity With Certain Properties

Example Prompt:
Find the root of unity highlighted in the diagram below.

[IMG: /graphics/98e9ea0ab66a999ba39a7d107f156d9f]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The [MATH: n]th roots of unity lie at the vertices of a regular [MATH: n]-gon inscribed inside the unit circle in the complex plane. One of the vertices of this regular [MATH: n]-gon must lie at the point [MATH: (1,0).]

Since there are [MATH: 7] points in our diagram, we need to find a [MATH: 7]th root of unity.

First, we express the complex number [MATH: 1] in the form [MATH: re^{\textrm{i}\theta}.] Notice that [MATH: |1| = 1] and [MATH: \arg(1) = 0.] Hence,

[MATH: 1 = e^{\textrm{i}(0 + 2k\pi)} = e^{2k\pi \textrm{i}},]

where [MATH: k] is an integer. So, we have

[MATH: z^{7} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}}⟹z = (e^{2kπ\textrm{i}})^{1/7} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/7}.]

To find the index [MATH: k] of our root of unity, we enumerate the roots in the diagram counter-clockwise, starting with the root at [MATH: (1,0)] corresponding to [MATH: k=0,] as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/047d35f0458fccba0e9e329b3fa9f8c2]

So, the required root corresponds to [MATH: k=5.] Substituting this into the expression for roots, we obtain the following:

[MATH: z_{5} = e^{2(5)π\textrm{i}/7} = e^{10π\textrm{i}/7}]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Closing Remark

Content:
Earlier, when finding the 5th roots of unity, we substituted the integers from [MATH: k=0] to [MATH: k=4] inclusive into the following formula:

Content:
[MATH: z_{k} = e^{2kπ\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
This process gave us the following results:

Content:
[MATH: z_0 = 1, \qquad z_1 = e^{2\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_2 = e^{4\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_3 = e^{6\pi\textrm{i}/5}, \qquad z_4 = e^{8\pi\textrm{i}/5}]

Content:
You may be wondering why we stopped at [MATH: k=4.] What about [MATH: k=5,6,7,\ldots?]

Content:
It turns out that if we continue substituting values for [MATH: k,] we'll get the same results repeated. In other words, we will not get any other roots.

Content:
For example, substituting [MATH: k=8] into our formula gives

Content:
[MATH: z_{8}|= e^{2(8)π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{16π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5 + 10π\textrm{i}/5}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5 + 2π\textrm{i}}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5} ⋅ e^{2π\textrm{i}}; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5} ⋅ 1; = e^{6π\textrm{i}/5}; = z_{3}.]
